title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 2: Legal Empowerment of the Poor
keywords: social justice, not just empty legalisms
primary_topics: Chapter 2 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3) -- CJP's July 29, 2007 Inquirer column arguing that the rule of law alone cannot help the poorest, who also need 'legal empowerment' and 'social justice,' opened by the story of 'Jose Cruz,' a teenage Makati newspaper vendor and informal settler

How extreme poverty turns the Bill of Rights into 'empty rhetoric': Jose and his sisters have no birth certificates, no legal residence, no title to their shanty-stall and no access to legal protection, social security, or the economy -- leaving them 'a hairline away from a life of crime and violence'

The conference on the 'legal exclusion of the poor' (ESCR-Asia, the UNDP, and the UN-affiliated Commission on Legal Empowerment for the Poor), which showed that 'orthodox' rule of law -- its courts, lawyers, fees and complex laws -- is 'alien to the day-to-day existence of the very poor'

CJP's 'awakening': that his 'twin vision of safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity' requires 'not just the rule of law but also the legal empowerment of the poor' -- with thanks to the conference organizers and the Commission co-chaired by Madeleine Albright and Hernando de Soto
sub_topics: Jose Cruz (not his real name): a boy 'barely in his teens' who wakes at 4 a.m. to sell newspapers at a busy Makati intersection, lives in an 'all-purpose shanty along the riles' on the South Super Highway, and helps his 'partly paralyzed mother' mind a makeshift sari-sari store, with no time for school, trade or skill

A family legally invisible: having migrated from Sorsogon, Jose and his two sisters are 'informal settlers' with no birth certificates (their mother 'too embarrassed' to admit an itinerant, already-married father), no legal residence, no title to their shack-stall, and no medical care for recurring sores
Raids and demolitions: their settlement has been raided by police and thugs hunting drugs or suspects, and their hut demolished so they could be 'banished from the view' of visiting foreign VIPs

The Bill of Rights as 'empty rhetoric': poverty and powerlessness deny Jose 'access to effective legal protection, to the social security system, and to integration into the economy,' leaving him near 'a life of crime and violence' and his sisters near 'prostitution and vagrancy'

The conference on legal exclusion: ESCR-Asia, with the UNDP and the UN-affiliated Commission on Legal Empowerment for the Poor, convened a July 25-26 national policy conference on 'the nature, dimensions and extent of the legal exclusion of the poor,' asking how the poorest can 'overcome the constraints that prevent them from accessing the legal system'

Why 'orthodox' rule of law falls short: its ideas, institutions (courts), officials (lawyers, prosecutors) and strategies are 'alien to the day-to-day existence of the very poor' -- laws are 'enacted without consulting them,' 'too complicated' for them to understand or invoke, and 'lawyers' fees and docket costs are beyond their means'

Jose's concrete legal disadvantages: he 'lacks legal status (he is a minor) and residence,' the mini-store 'is not registered and thus has no permit,' and he knows of no lawyer who 'would waste time to protect their insignificant livelihood'

From rule of law to legal empowerment: society has 'a big stake' in keeping Jose's family from sliding 'from the legally excluded poor to socially condemned criminals,' so they need 'legal empowerment, not just the rule of law' and 'social justice, not just empty legalisms' -- an 'awakening' that, for CJP, makes 'liberty and prosperity for all' depend on legally empowering the poor (with thanks to Glenda Litong, Resurreccion Lao, and Dr. Naresh Singh, and the Commission co-chaired by Madeleine Albright and Hernando de Soto)

stances.claim: For the poorest, the Bill of Rights is 'empty rhetoric': extreme poverty and powerlessness deny them access to legal protection, social security and the economy, so 'orthodox' rule of law -- built on courts, lawyers, fees and complex laws 'alien to the day-to-day existence of the very poor' -- 'cannot adequately help them.'
stances.rhetorical_move: narrative-then-indictment: using Jose Cruz's story to expose the rule of law's blind spot for the excluded

stances.claim: The poor need 'legal empowerment, not just the rule of law' and 'social justice, not just empty legalisms' -- both to protect their rights and to keep them from degenerating 'from the legally excluded poor to socially condemned criminals,' a stake the whole society shares.
stances.rhetorical_move: reframing: elevating legal empowerment above formal legality as the real remedy

stances.claim: CJP's own 'awakening': having long believed the rule of law sufficed for his 'twin vision of safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity,' he is now 'convinced' that 'liberty and prosperity for all requires not just the rule of law but also the legal empowerment of the poor.'

notable_anecdotes: Jose Cruz at 4 a.m.: CJP opens with the pseudonymous boy who rises before dawn to peddle newspapers at a Makati intersection and breakfasts on 'boiled rice mixed with condensed milk' before minding a sari-sari store with his partly paralyzed mother.

No papers at all: he details how the family has no birth certificates, no residence, no title and no permit -- legally invisible -- and how their hut was demolished to hide them from 'visiting foreign VIPs.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3), CJP's July 29, 2007 Inquirer column, argues that the rule of law alone cannot rescue the poorest, who also need 'legal empowerment' and 'social justice.' He opens with 'Jose Cruz' (a pseudonym), a boy 'barely in his teens' who wakes at 4 a.m. to sell newspapers at a Makati intersection, lives in 'an all-purpose shanty along the riles' on the South Super Highway, and helps his 'partly paralyzed mother' mind a makeshift store, with no time for school or skill. Having migrated from Sorsogon, Jose and his two sisters are 'informal settlers' with no birth certificates, no legal residence, no title to their shack-stall and no medical care -- legally invisible, their hut once demolished so they could be 'banished from the view' of visiting foreign VIPs. For such a family, CJP writes, the Bill of Rights is 'empty rhetoric,' because poverty denies 'access to effective legal protection, to the social security system, and to integration into the economy,' leaving Jose 'a hairline away from a life of crime and violence.' Drawing on a July 25-26 conference convened by ESCR-Asia with the UNDP and the UN-affiliated Commission on Legal Empowerment for the Poor on 'the legal exclusion of the poor,' he explains why 'orthodox' rule of law fails them: its courts, lawyers, fees and complex laws are 'alien to the day-to-day existence of the very poor,' who are not consulted when laws are made and cannot afford to invoke them. Jose's disadvantages are concrete -- no legal status (he is a minor), an unregistered store, and no lawyer willing to help. Because society has 'a big stake' in keeping such families from sliding 'from the legally excluded poor to socially condemned criminals,' they need 'legal empowerment, not just the rule of law' and 'social justice, not just empty legalisms.' The conference, he says, produced an 'awakening': a jurist who long thought the rule of law sufficient for his 'twin vision of safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity' now believes 'liberty and prosperity for all requires not just the rule of law but also the legal empowerment of the poor' -- thanking organizers Glenda Litong, Resurreccion Lao and Dr. Naresh Singh, and noting the Commission's co-chairs, Madeleine Albright and Hernando de Soto.
